title: Binary and Data Representation (KS4 Computer Science)
subject: Computer Science
strapline: How computers store everything as 1s and 0s.
facts: Computers use binary (base 2) — only two digits, 0 and 1 — because circuits are either off or on.
A single binary digit is a bit; 8 bits make a byte.
Place values in an 8-bit byte are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
To convert binary to denary, add the place values wherever there is a 1: 00001010 = 8 + 2 = 10.
Storage units go up in powers: 1000 bytes ≈ 1 kilobyte, 1000 KB ≈ 1 megabyte, then gigabyte, terabyte.
Text is stored using character sets such as ASCII (each character has a binary code).
Images are stored as pixels; more bits per pixel (colour depth) and more pixels (resolution) mean a bigger file.

quick_quiz.q: How many bits are in a byte?
What number system uses only 0 and 1?

teacher_tips: Practise conversions both ways using the place-value headings.
Relate file size to colour depth and resolution with real examples.
Use physical bit cards (flip 0/1) to make binary hands-on.
